question: When a machine takes over the core task of a job, does the job disappear, or does the name stay while the work moves on, and can today's newest workers move on with it the way earlier ones did?

issues.note: Narration moves to the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and spacecraft, but the picture is the generic Langley pencil-and-graph desk. The change of place is not shown, and the abstract desk does not match the narration.

Narration moves to the second job title, software developers, over the same dark office and lamp desk as the programmers section. Nothing in the picture marks the switch to a second job, so the two directions are hard to tell apart.

The film jumps from the dark modern office to a warm 1940s pencil desk, split with the code screen, for 'checking the machine's numbers'. The look is a hard mix of two eras, though the point of it is understandable.
Cut to a near-empty dark office for 'the people just starting out'. The picture shows no beginners, only an empty room.
A long dark archive corridor appears for 'the second kind of work'. It is not yet tied to programming and reads as an abstract jump.
The same dim office and lamp desk, with slow camera drifts, runs from about R09.3 to R09.6. That is roughly 12 s of near-identical picture.
From R10.4 to R11.3 the dark empty office and desk wide shot repeats with almost no change while the statistics run.
The same dark office and the same dark-office wide shot repeat across R12.5, R12.6, R13.1 and R13.2 (Stanford section). The only new element is overlay text.
The pencil desk with the lamp and the same desk angle recurs across R05.3 to R05.8 and again in the JPL section. It feels repetitive.
